# Federated learning with blockchain commitments for medical prediction: results draft

*Generated by `python3 -m fedverify.analysis.make_results_draft` from the results files; do not edit by hand. Comparisons: RESULTS_DRAFT.comparisons.json.*

## Experimental Setup

### A. Data

**UCI heart disease.** 920 rows from 4 hospitals (the `dataset` column); label: heart disease present. Paper mode drops the columns ca, thal and slope and then every incomplete row (180 rows), leaving 740 patients, 383 with heart disease: Cleveland 304 (139 positive), Hungary 260 (98 positive), VA Long Beach 130 (101 positive), Switzerland 46 (45 positive).

**TCGA-BRCA.** 907 cases in the clinical workbook; the 5 largest source sites are the hospitals: 474 patients and 76 deaths (BH 145 (45 deaths), A2 98 (11 deaths), E2 87 (6 deaths), A8 76 (4 deaths), AR 68 (10 deaths)). Binary task: the death indicator. Survival task: time to death or censoring with an accelerated-failure-time model, follow-up below 1.0 day clipped up to it (11 patients).

Preprocessing fits nothing on patients: fixed scaling constants and a fixed one-hot vocabulary, 23 encoded features for heart and 30 for TCGA-BRCA.

### B. Protocol

Repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation, strata (hospital, label), 5 repeats with seeds 0–4; every hospital trains only on its own rows. Each method runs 30 rounds and is evaluated after every round; the final-round out-of-fold predictions of all folds are pooled and every metric is computed once per repeat, then summarised as mean ± std over the repeats. Metrics: Accuracy, F1, ROC-AUC (heart); C-index, ROC-AUC, F1 (TCGA-BRCA, plus accuracy computed from the out-of-fold predictions). F1: threshold maximising F1 on the training fold's predictions (each hospital's own threshold for local_* methods), applied to that fold's test patients. Accuracy uses the same threshold as f1 (phase 7): the threshold maximising f1 on the training fold's predictions, for the pooled, per-hospital and per-round train/test accuracy alike.

### C. Models and federation

Logistic regression: 3 local epochs per round, batch 32, SGD learning rate 0.1, class-weighted loss; FedSGD takes one full-batch step per round and FedAvg averages the hospitals' deltas weighted by sample count. Random forest: 10 trees per hospital per round, depth 5, minimum leaf 3; the federated forest concatenates every hospital's trees. XGBoost: 5 new trees per hospital per round, depth 3, learning rate 0.1, subsample 0.8, aggregated by FedXGBBagging (every hospital boosts from the broadcast global margin; the server keeps all new trees and adds the average of the round's new boosters over the contributing hospitals to the global margin, a correction made after the held-out log-loss curves showed that summing them overshoots). Local-only models score each patient with their own hospital's model; centralized training pools every hospital's rows with the same budget.

Differential privacy (logistic model only): DP-SGD with target ε in 1, 2, 4, 8, ∞ (∞ = no DP), δ = 1e-05, clipping norm 1.0, sigma solved once over all steps of a fold-run. Blockchain-FL (commit only) serializes every update without pickle, gives it a content ID, signs it with the hospital's Ed25519 key (test keys), verifies it, commits the round as a Merkle root and anchors the root; the server aggregates the updates rebuilt from the committed bytes. Sweeps use the mock anchor; one run per dataset mines blocks on the existing proof-of-work chain (difficulty 2). Ours adds screening to that pipeline (and DP to the logistic model).

### D. Attacks and screening

One of the K hospitals is malicious (1 per repeat), chosen by attacks.byzantine.attacker_ids on the repeat seed, attacker_frac=1/K, from the first round, with non-adaptive attacks: sign_flip, scaling and label_flip for the logistic model, label_flip_trees and random_trees for the tree models. The logistic screen is the existing FedVerify-Forensics aggregator; the tree screen compares each hospital's new trees on a public probe set of 512 schema rows (no patient data) by a robust z of the distance to the median prediction. tau is never set by hand: it comes from a calibration at seed 1000 (80 cells, 30 rounds, 5 folds; every hospital in turn plays the attacker), policy tau_fpr5 (the highest detection rate at a false-positive rate of at most 5% on the calibration rounds).

The reference paper's three blockchain attacks are simulated against our commit layer: every simulated round is a real commit round plus one attack attempt, 100 rounds per attack and dataset at seed 0, the variant and target drawn from the seed. Resilience S is the share of rounds in which the defence held, as the reference paper defines it.

## Results

Comparisons follow one rule (Phase 11): method A outperforms method B only if the 95% patient-level bootstrap confidence interval of their paired difference excludes 0 (both run on the same folds and repeats; 2000 resamples of the patients, stratified by hospital, fixed seed); otherwise they are not distinguishable at this sample size. The mean paired difference ± its standard deviation over the repeats is reported with each interval. No p-values are given: with 5 repeats an exact test cannot go below 0.0625.

**UCI heart disease, ROC-AUC.** Logistic regression: federated training (0.859 ± 0.001) is outperformed by centralized training (0.866 ± 0.002) and outperforms local-only models (0.837 ± 0.002); ours (0.856 ± 0.003) is not distinguishable at this sample size from vanilla FL. Random forest: federated training (0.864 ± 0.002) is outperformed by centralized training (0.879 ± 0.000) and is not distinguishable at this sample size from local-only models (0.869 ± 0.004); ours (0.866 ± 0.002) is not ranked against vanilla FL; screening a clean run excludes 13.3% of honest hospital-rounds (above 5.0%), so any gain may come from dropping a skewed hospital's updates rather than from catching attackers. XGBoost: federated training (0.843 ± 0.005) is not distinguishable at this sample size from centralized training (0.846 ± 0.003) and is not distinguishable at this sample size from local-only models (0.839 ± 0.009); ours (0.838 ± 0.005) is outperformed by vanilla FL.

**TCGA-BRCA, C-index.** Logistic regression: federated training (0.574 ± 0.019) is not distinguishable at this sample size from centralized training (0.576 ± 0.020) and is not distinguishable at this sample size from local-only models (0.539 ± 0.017); ours (0.517 ± 0.038) is not distinguishable at this sample size from vanilla FL. Random forest: federated training (0.674 ± 0.012) outperforms centralized training (0.616 ± 0.009) — but this gap was not diagnosed: Phase 8 diagnosed XGBoost only, and the random forest has no step-matched row; the centralized random forest's pooled held-out C-index is 0.615 after round 1 and 0.616 after round 30 — and is not distinguishable at this sample size from local-only models (0.635 ± 0.013); ours (0.669 ± 0.015) is outperformed by vanilla FL. XGBoost AFT: federated training (0.637 ± 0.010) outperforms centralized training (0.565 ± 0.016) — but centralized XGBoost over-fits (Phase 8: over the 30 rounds its training C-index rises from 0.830 to 0.993 while its held-out C-index falls from 0.666 to 0.565), and federated training is not distinguishable at this sample size from the step-matched centralized row (+0.037, 95% CI -0.002 to +0.075) — and is not distinguishable at this sample size from local-only models (0.650 ± 0.020); ours (0.626 ± 0.009) is not distinguishable at this sample size from vanilla FL.

**TCGA-BRCA, accuracy.** Predict all alive (baseline) scores ROC-AUC 0.500 ± 0.000, F1 0.000 ± 0.000, Accuracy 0.840 ± 0.000, ROC-AUC within hospital 0.500 ± 0.000; its accuracy is the majority-class rate (0.840). The accuracies in the binary table range from 0.510 to 0.809: 0 of 17 exceed that rate by more than 0.01, 0 lie within 0.01 of it (never ranked) and the rest are below it; no method's accuracy beats predicting everyone alive, and accuracy does not separate the TCGA-BRCA methods from the trivial model; ROC-AUC, F1 and the C-index are the informative metrics there. Accuracy uses the F1 threshold (fitted on the training fold), which trades accuracy for finding deaths; the per-round accuracy curves used P(event) ≥ 0.5 before Phase 7 and sat close to each hospital's majority-class rate, which is why accuracy and F1 looked as if they used different thresholds: they did.

**Reference rows.** Centralized XGBoost over-fits: on TCGA-BRCA its AFT model reaches a training C-index of 0.993 while its held-out C-index is 0.565 (DESIGN_NOTES.md section 8); the step-matched diagnostic row, which takes the federated model's 150 boosting steps and was not a blind result, reaches 0.600 ± 0.020. Scoring each patient by nothing but their hospital's training-fold event rate gives a pooled ROC-AUC of 0.700 ± 0.000 on TCGA-BRCA (UCI heart disease: 0.674 ± 0.000), so pooled ROC-AUC partly measures how base rates differ between hospitals. UCI heart disease (methods_heart), against the site-rate reference (0.674 ± 0.000): on ROC-AUC, all 17 exceed it (95% CI of the paired difference above 0); none is below it. TCGA-BRCA (methods_tcga_binary), against the site-rate reference (0.700 ± 0.000): on ROC-AUC, none exceeds it; 12 of 17 are below it (95% CI below 0); the other 5 are not distinguishable from it (Random forest: Local; XGBoost: Local; Random forest: Vanilla FL; Random forest: Blockchain-FL (commit only); Random forest: Ours). TCGA-BRCA (methods_tcga_binary), against the site-rate reference (0.407 ± 0.000): on F1, none exceeds it; 15 of 17 are below it (95% CI below 0); the other 2 are not distinguishable from it (Random forest: Local; XGBoost: Local). TCGA-BRCA (methods_tcga_survival), against the site-rate reference (0.585 ± 0.002): on C-index, none exceeds it; none is below it; all 17 are not distinguishable from it.

**Within hospital.** Pooled ROC-AUC and C-index compare patients from different hospitals too, so part of what they measure is how outcome rates differ between hospitals. The method tables therefore also give both metrics within hospital: each hospital's own out-of-fold patients, combined weighted by their comparable pairs (left out, fewer than 5 of the rarer class: Switzerland (1 negative); A8 (4 deaths)). The highest score is compared with the runner-up by the same paired interval as every other comparison (a run with identical predictions, such as a commit-only twin, is not a runner-up). UCI heart disease (methods_heart), ROC-AUC within hospital: highest score Random forest: Centralized at 0.864 ± 0.001 (pooled 0.879 ± 0.000), not distinguishable from Random forest: Ours (0.860 ± 0.002; paired difference +0.003, 95% CI -0.003 to +0.010); the site-rate reference scores 0.493 ± 0.000. TCGA-BRCA (methods_tcga_binary), ROC-AUC within hospital: highest score Random forest: Vanilla FL at 0.646 ± 0.015 (pooled 0.613 ± 0.013), not distinguishable from Random forest: Ours (0.641 ± 0.019; paired difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.000 to +0.009) (Random forest: Blockchain-FL (commit only) scores the same, with identical predictions); the site-rate reference scores 0.488 ± 0.000. TCGA-BRCA (methods_tcga_survival), C-index within hospital: highest score Random forest: Vanilla FL at 0.666 ± 0.012 (pooled 0.674 ± 0.012), not distinguishable from Random forest: Ours (0.660 ± 0.015; paired difference +0.005, 95% CI -0.000 to +0.011) (Random forest: Blockchain-FL (commit only) scores the same, with identical predictions); the site-rate reference scores 0.485 ± 0.005. A score that is constant within a hospital gets exactly 0.5 there (Predict all alive does); the site-rate reference falls slightly below 0.5 because its rate is computed on the other folds, so it differs a little between folds whenever a hospital's events do not split evenly over them, which ranks a fold's own events slightly lower.

- Paired difference A − B: per repeat, both on the same folds; mean ± sample std over the repeats. 95% CI: 2000 patient-level bootstrap resamples, stratified by hospital (seed 0), of the mean over repeats of the difference. Verdict: A outperforms B only if the CI excludes 0. No p-values (with 5 repeats an exact test cannot go below 0.0625).
- The CI holds the trained runs fixed and resamples patients; it does not include the variation between training runs. † marks the comparisons whose std over repeats exceeds half the CI width (0 of 28): there, training randomness matters more than patient sampling, and the CI alone overstates certainty.
- Not ranked (Phase 7): where the screen of Ours excludes more than 5.0% of honest hospital-rounds on a clean run, a gain of Ours is not written as outperforming: it may come from dropping a skewed hospital's updates rather than from catching attackers.
- Federated gains over centralized training on TCGA-BRCA (Phase 12) carry, in the same cell, what the Phase 8 diagnosis of the centralized model found (DESIGN_NOTES.md section 8) and how federated training (A) compares with the step-matched centralized row, from that comparison's own interval; for a model the diagnosis did not cover, the cell says so.

**Paired comparisons.** Of the 20 federated-versus-baseline and ours-versus-federated comparisons in the table above, 9 have a 95% bootstrap interval that excludes 0 and 8 of those are ranked; the others are not distinguishable at this sample size. UCI heart disease, random forest: the gain of Ours over Vanilla FL (+0.003, 95% CI +0.000 to +0.006) is not ranked: screening a clean run excludes 13.3% of honest hospital-rounds (above 5.0%), so any gain may come from dropping a skewed hospital's updates rather than from catching attackers. TCGA-BRCA, random forest: Vanilla FL outperforms Centralized (+0.058, 95% CI +0.013 to +0.104), but this gap was not diagnosed: Phase 8 diagnosed XGBoost only, and the random forest has no step-matched row; the centralized random forest's pooled held-out C-index is 0.615 after round 1 and 0.616 after round 30. TCGA-BRCA, XGBoost AFT: Vanilla FL outperforms Centralized (+0.072, 95% CI +0.023 to +0.122), but centralized XGBoost over-fits (Phase 8: over the 30 rounds its training C-index rises from 0.830 to 0.993 while its held-out C-index falls from 0.666 to 0.565), and federated training is not distinguishable at this sample size from the step-matched centralized row (+0.037, 95% CI -0.002 to +0.075). TCGA-BRCA intervals are wide because its 76 deaths give few comparable pairs, so most TCGA differences, even large ones, cannot be ranked. The interval resamples patients with the trained runs held fixed; the std over repeats beside it shows how much the training runs themselves vary.

### F. Blockchain attacks

**Table (chain_resilience). Chain-attack resilience (Figs 9 and 10)**


Resilience of the commit layer to the reference paper's three blockchain attacks: 100 simulated rounds per attack, seed 0.

| Attack | Metric | UCI heart disease (K = 4): S (%) | UCI heart disease (K = 4): Success (%) | UCI heart disease (K = 4): S, defences off (%) | TCGA-BRCA (K = 5): S (%) | TCGA-BRCA (K = 5): Success (%) | TCGA-BRCA (K = 5): S, defences off (%) | Reported: Myrzashova et al. (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Double spending | S_DS | 100.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 100.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 91 |
| Transaction malleability | S_TM | 100.0 | 0.0 | 8.0 | 100.0 | 0.0 | 5.0 | 88 |
| Endpoint compromise | S_EC | 100.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 100.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 81 |

- S = rounds in which the defence held / simulated rounds × 100; attack success = 100 − S (the reference paper's definitions). Each round is one real commit round of our pipeline plus one attack attempt, with the variant and target drawn from the seed. Defences off: the defences of that attack switched off (tests show each simulated variant then lands).
- 100% here holds by construction: each simulated variant meets a deterministic check (a signature, a counter, a slot, a Merkle root) that it cannot pass, so the number says which variants are covered, not how often a defence fails. It is not comparable with the reference paper's reported double spending 91%, transaction malleability 88%, endpoint compromise 81%, which come from a different system and simulation.
- Covered (simulated): Double spending: conflicting update, replayed submission, stale update respent, duplicate resubmission; Transaction malleability: timestamp changed, txn id changed, leaf order swapped; Endpoint compromise: unregistered key, forged signature, wrong hospital key, key reregistration.
- Not covered: Double spending: forks and chain reorganisations (51% attacks), equivocation across several aggregators or ledgers, re-use of an update from another run by its own hospital; Transaction malleability: reordering submissions in transit, before the root is built, dropping or delaying submissions; Endpoint compromise: a stolen private key, multi-factor authentication and firewalls (not simulated), key revocation and rotation.
- Our proof-of-work difficulty is 2 on one local node, so our blocks take milliseconds; the reference paper reports about 5 s per block (the baseline of its Fig 7). Block times and latencies are not comparable between the two.

XGBoost: screening a clean run excludes 9.0% of honest hospital-rounds (above 5.0%), so any gain may come from dropping a skewed hospital's updates rather than from catching attackers. Under label_flip_trees, the screened run (0.640 ± 0.026) is not distinguishable at this sample size from the unscreened one (0.621 ± 0.050); the screen caught 98.8% of attacker rounds (recall) with precision 91.4%, against a clean false-exclusion rate of 9.0%. Under random_trees, the screened run (0.651 ± 0.028) is not ranked against the unscreened one (0.640 ± 0.028); the screen caught 18.0% of attacker rounds (recall) with precision 45.2%, against a clean false-exclusion rate of 9.0%.

**TCGA-BRCA (attack_tcga_survival), C-index.** XGBoost AFT: screening a clean run excludes 12.2% of honest hospital-rounds (above 5.0%), so any gain may come from dropping a skewed hospital's updates rather than from catching attackers. Under label_flip_trees, the screened run (0.632 ± 0.019) is not distinguishable at this sample size from the unscreened one (0.627 ± 0.021); the screen caught 58.8% of attacker rounds (recall) with precision 81.7%, against a clean false-exclusion rate of 12.2%. Screen recall is low: with K = 4 hospitals, recall on UCI heart disease is 13–27% over every attack and model; with K = 5 hospitals, recall on TCGA-BRCA is 9–99% over every attack and model. Most attacker hospital-rounds are not excluded, so the screen limits rather than prevents poisoning.

## Limitations

- TCGA-BRCA has only 76 deaths among 474 patients; A8 has 4, too few for a per-hospital C-index or AUC, and the pooled C-index of every method in the survival table lies between 0.517 and 0.674.
- The heart hospitals are small and unbalanced in paper mode (Cleveland 304 rows, 139 positive, Hungary 260 rows, 98 positive, VA Long Beach 130 rows, 101 positive, Switzerland 46 rows, 45 positive); Switzerland has 1 negative among 46 rows, so it gets no local-only model and per-hospital rank metrics there are undefined.
- The proof-of-work chain is simulated: one local node in one process (the existing BlockVerify chain, difficulty 2), the sweeps use the mock anchor, and latency, throughput and send rate are single-machine wall-clock values, not a network's. No consortium or public chain, no FPoW (undefined), no homomorphic encryption.
- Attackers are non-adaptive and at most 1 of K; the median/MAD screens cannot handle collusion, and the public probe set could be gamed by an attacker who knows it. tau is calibrated on the same attack families.
- Screening on heart is weak: the calibration ROC-AUC of the heart screens lies between 0.638 and 0.689, with hospitals that differ strongly in size and outcome rate (Section A); screening clean runs excludes honest hospitals more often than the calibration target (attack tables, 'Clean false excl.' column). Screen recall is low: with K = 4 hospitals, recall on UCI heart disease is 13–27% over every attack and model; with K = 5 hospitals, recall on TCGA-BRCA is 9–99% over every attack and model. Most attacker hospital-rounds are not excluded, so the screen limits rather than prevents poisoning.
- TCGA centralized XGBoost (AFT C-index 0.565, death-indicator ROC-AUC 0.540) is below local (0.650, 0.691) and federated XGBoost (0.637, 0.600) because it over-fits, and federated XGBoost is not distinguishable at this sample size from the step-matched centralized row on C-index (+0.037, 95% CI -0.002 to +0.075) and is not distinguishable at this sample size from it on ROC-AUC (+0.037, 95% CI -0.007 to +0.079). The centralized model's training C-index rises from 0.830 to 0.993 (binary training ROC-AUC 0.813 to 1.000) while its held-out C-index falls overall, from 0.666 after round 1 to 0.565 after round 30. It holds as many trees as the federated model (750), but adds 25 sequential boosting steps per round against 5 for the federated model (whose round boosters are averaged since Phase 7) and for local models: 750 against 150 after the last round. At the same 150 steps it scores 0.602, so the step count explains part of the gap; no gap beyond it is shown: on the C-index neither federated XGBoost (above) nor local (+0.050, 95% CI -0.007 to +0.114) is distinguishable from the step-matched row. Run as its own diagnostic row (rule fixed in table.yaml after this diagnosis, so not a blind result), the step-matched centralized model reaches 0.600 ± 0.020 (C-index) and 0.563 ± 0.012 (ROC-AUC). Site event rates (death rate 5–31% by site) explain local's lead on pairs of patients from different sites (local: 0.666 on cross-site pairs, 0.601 within sites; a predictor that knows only the site's death rate reaches 0.585, and its ROC-AUC 0.700 is not below local's death-indicator ROC-AUC), not central's drop: within hospital (C-index, by the paired rule), where site rates cannot help, federated XGBoost outperforms the over-fitted central model (+0.068, 95% CI +0.017 to +0.119) and is not distinguishable at this sample size from the step-matched row (+0.033, 95% CI -0.009 to +0.075), and local is not distinguishable at this sample size from central (+0.048, 95% CI -0.004 to +0.102). The equal-tree budget is a documented design choice, not a configuration bug, so it was not changed after seeing these results (results/diagnostics/central_xgb_tcga.json; DESIGN_NOTES.md section 8).
- On TCGA-BRCA, predicting every patient alive already reaches accuracy 0.840 (the majority-class rate), so accuracy there says almost nothing about a model; the draft does not rank accuracies within 0.01 of the majority-class rate.
- DP is per training example (record-level), not per patient or per hospital; each fold-run is accounted separately; the tree models (random forest, XGBoost) have no DP at all, so their trees reveal split thresholds and leaf statistics of patient data to the server.
- Uncertainty: every ranking rests on a 95% patient-level bootstrap interval of a paired difference over 5 repeats of cross-validation on the same data. The interval holds the trained runs fixed, so it omits the variation between training runs (reported separately as the std over repeats), and it is not a test across datasets. No p-values are reported: with 5 repeats an exact test cannot go below 0.0625. VERDICT_CHANGES.md lists every verdict whose wording changed from the earlier mean ± std rule.
- Keys are test keys derived from the run seed, timestamps are a logical clock, and the chain-attack resilience comes from one simulation per dataset.
